summary: Players alternately take a number from either end of the array; does player 1 end with at least as much as player 2?
mainInsight: Define dp[i][j] as the best score difference (current player minus the opponent) on the subarray i..j. The current player takes either end and the opponent then plays optimally: dp[i][j] = max(nums[i] - dp[i + 1][j], nums[j] - dp[i][j - 1]). Player 1 wins iff dp[0][n - 1] >= 0.

approaches.name: Minimax recursion
approaches.summary: Try both ends at each turn with exponential branching.

commonMistakes: Adding instead of subtracting the opponent's value
edgeCases: Even length arrays (player 1 always wins in the Stone Game variant)

cards.answer: The best score difference (mover minus opponent) on the subarray i..j
cards.explanation: A zero-sum game: what you gain is what the opponent loses.

incorrectOptionExplanations.The plain sum of the numbers from index: That is a prefix sum quantity.

promptVariants: Why does the recurrence subtract dp of the sub-problem?
cards.answer: After the mover takes an end, the opponent becomes the mover on the smaller range and obtains dp[...] difference in their favour. From the original mover's view that difference counts against them, so the result is nums[end] - dp[remaining]. Taking the max over both ends gives optimal play.
cards.explanation: Player 1 wins on dp[0][n-1] >= 0 (ties go to player 1).
